content:
Warren Buffett is donating about $5.47 billion of Berkshire Hathaway shares to four charities run by his family, the 96-year-old investor said on Monday, in the largest single Thanksgiving gift of his two-decade campaign to give away his fortune.

Buffett announced the donation in his annual Thanksgiving message to Berkshire shareholders, converting 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares for the gift, according to Reuters. Valued at Berkshire's closing price of $592.94 per Class B share on Friday, November 13, the donation is worth approximately $5.47 billion — more than four times the size of his Thanksgiving gift in 2025.

The shares will be divided among four foundations led by his adult children. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after his late first wife, will receive the largest share — 3,690,000 shares, or 40 percent of the total gift. The Sherwood Foundation, the Howard G. Buffett Foundation and the NoVo Foundation will each receive 1,845,000 shares. The foundations are overseen by his children Susie, 73, Howard, 71, and Peter, 68.

The four foundations work in very different fields, and the split reflects that. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation focuses on reproductive health and rights around the world and funds college scholarships for students in Buffett's home state of Nebraska. The Sherwood Foundation supports non-profit organisations in Nebraska, the Howard G. Buffett Foundation works on global food security, and the NoVo Foundation backs programmes for women and girls. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, which has received more than $47 billion of Berkshire stock from Buffett since 2006, was not included in this latest donation.

With Monday's gift, Buffett has now given more than $29 billion of Berkshire stock to the four family foundations, according to Reuters. The pace of his giving has accelerated sharply this year: including a separate donation of nearly $6 billion in July, he has handed the four charities roughly $11.4 billion in 2026 alone. That speed is the point — Buffett has said he wants his remaining Berkshire shares distributed by the end of 2034, a firm deadline he set out earlier this year.

The announcement also carried a message about the company he built over six decades. Buffett said his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway remains "as strong as ever", a pointed reassurance in his first Thanksgiving letter since handing over as chief executive to Greg Abel at the start of this year. Abel now runs the conglomerate day to day, while Buffett remains chairman, and the letter was read on Wall Street as an endorsement of the succession he spent years preparing.

That is the gap most of the early coverage of the gift left open. Wire reports led with the dollar figure, but the real story of this year's letter is the handover: the world's most famous investor is no longer running the company, and he is using his annual message to tell shareholders the business is in safe hands. Buffett built Berkshire from a struggling textile mill into one of the world's most valuable companies, and his fortune — almost all of it in Berkshire stock — is the raw material of the largest private philanthropic programme in history.

The scale is difficult to overstate. Few individuals have ever given away money at this rate: $11.4 billion in a single year to four family-run foundations, on top of more than $47 billion to the Gates Foundation since 2006, puts Buffett's lifetime giving well past $85 billion. Unlike most billionaire philanthropy, the money is not parked in a foundation bearing his name to be spent decades from now — it goes to charities his children already run, with a deadline to finish the job by 2034.

What the foundations do next with the shares matters as much as the headline number. The Sherwood and Susan Thompson Buffett foundations concentrate much of their spending in Nebraska, where Buffett has lived all his life, while the Howard G. Buffett Foundation funds food-security work in conflict zones and the NoVo Foundation supports women and girls globally. The [Times of India reported](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/us/twenty-years-after-warren-buffett-began-giving-away-his-fortune-the-96-year-old-investor-has-announced-another-5-47-billion-gift-to-four-family-foundations-taking-his-giving-to-those-charities-past-29-billion/articleshow/135892958.cms) that the latest gift takes his donations to the four foundations past $29 billion, around 20 years after he first started giving his fortune away.

The gift comes in a week of heavyweight deal-making elsewhere in the world economy. In Shenzhen, China and Canada agreed to deepen tariff relief on hundreds of millions of dollars of trade, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-carney-tariff-cuts-shenzhen-november-2026), while Japan's economy contracted in the third quarter, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/japan-economy-contracts-q3-2026). Buffett's donation is a reminder that the same week can also be measured in what the world's richest people choose to give away, not only in what governments negotiate.

What happens next is, by now, a familiar rhythm. Buffett's Thanksgiving letter has become an annual event for Berkshire shareholders, and each year's gift has grown larger as the 2034 deadline approaches. The test for 2027 will be whether the foundations can put the money to work as fast as Buffett is giving it — and whether Berkshire, under Abel, keeps generating the returns that made the fortune worth giving away in the first place.
summary: Warren Buffett is donating about $5.47 billion of Berkshire Hathaway shares to four family foundations, he said on Monday, taking his gifts to those charities past $29 billion and reaffirming his confidence in the company he built over 60 years.
title: Warren Buffett donates $5.47 billion in Berkshire shares to family foundations
